claim: Motor fatigability emerges when demanding tasks are executed over an extended period of time.
source: Motor fatigability emerges when demanding tasks are executed over an extended period of time.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Motor slowing is associated with a gradual increase of net excitability in the motor network and, specifically, in primary motor cortex (M1), which results from overall disinhibition.
source: We show that motor slowing is associated with a gradual increase of net excitability in the motor network and, specifically, in primary motor cortex (M1), which results from overall disinhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI, EEG, and TMS data presented in the manuscript showing increased activity and decreased inhibition in M1.

claim: Performance decrements are linked to a breakdown of surround inhibition in M1, which is associated with high coactivation of antagonistic muscle groups.
source: Importantly, we link performance decrements to a breakdown of surround inhibition in M1, which is associated with high coactivation of antagonistic muscle groups.
evidence: This is supported by TMS measurements of surround inhibition and EMG measurements of muscle coactivation in experiment 9.

claim: A loss of inhibitory control might broaden the tuning of population vectors such that movement patterns become more variable, ill-timed and effortful.
source: This is consistent with the model that a loss of inhibitory control might broaden the tuning of population vectors such that movement patterns become more variable, ill-timed and effortful.
evidence: This is a theoretical model proposed to explain the experimental findings.

claim: The release of inhibition in M1 is an important mechanism underpinning motor fatigability and, potentially, also pathological fatigue as frequently observed in patients with brain disorders.
source: We propose that the release of inhibition in M1 is an important mechanism underpinning motor fatigability and, potentially, also pathological fatigue as frequently observed in patients with brain disorders.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings, with speculation about clinical implications.

claim: Enhanced motor fatigability is a prevalent symptom of many brain disorders (such as stroke, Parkinson's disease, or traumatic brain injury).
source: Enhanced motor fatigability is a prevalent symptom of many brain disorders (such as stroke, Parkinson's disease, or traumatic brain injury), which typically affects submaximal movements that are required for many daily life tasks (Kluger et al., 2013; Manjaly et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fatigability arises, at least partly, at the supraspinal level suggesting that the descending drive from motor cortex is suboptimal once it is fatigued.
source: In addition to clinical data, experimental evidence in healthy participants has shown that fatigability arises, at least partly, at the supraspinal level suggesting that the descending drive from motor cortex is suboptimal once it is fatigued (Gandevia et al., 1996; Smith et al., 2007; Søgaard et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: The performance of repetitive movements tends to deteriorate over time.
source: It has been demonstrated previously that the performance of repetitive movements tends to deteriorate over time (Dolan and Adams, 1998; Miller et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 7–9 s of finger tapping at the maximal voluntary rate is sufficient to induce a significant performance decrease.
source: For example, 7–9 s of finger tapping at the maximal voluntary rate is sufficient to induce a significant performance decrease (Aoki et al., 2003; Rodrigues et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Motor slowing is robustly evoked by prolonged finger tapping at high speed but markers of peripheral or muscular fatigability are virtually unchanged.
source: Previous studies have shown that motor slowing is robustly evoked by prolonged finger tapping at high speed but markers of peripheral or muscular fatigability are virtually unchanged (Arias et al., 2015; Madrid et al., 2016; Rodrigues et al., 2009), giving rise to the hypothesis that supraspinal mechanisms play a major role in evoking this phenomenon.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Slowed motor execution is a hallmark of healthy aging.
source: Moreover, slowed motor execution is a hallmark of healthy aging (Mattay et al., 2002; Yordanova et al., 2004) and associated with a dysregulation of motor cortex excitability (Teo et al., 2012a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Motor slowing starts immediately with movement onset and reaches a 'plateau' after approximately 30 s.
source: Calculating movement speed within 1 s bins revealed a characteristic speed reduction (slowing) which manifests immediately after movement onset and reaches a 'plateau' after approximately 30 s (Figure 1A), demonstrating that motor slowing is a time-dependent phenomenon which is only mildly expressed after the first 10 s while the full slowing effect is observed after 30 s.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A from experiment 1.

claim: A pronounced expression of slowing is only observed for high tapping speeds while paced tapping at lower speeds causes virtually no slowing.
source: Importantly, a pronounced expression of slowing is only observed for high tapping speeds while paced tapping at lower speeds causes virtually no slowing (Figure 1B, significant condition x time interaction (F(6,121)=49.314, p<0.001), supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from experiment 2 shown in Figure 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: Motor slowing is a gradual process which depends inherently on the initial speed and the time it is maintained.
source: Together experiment 1 and 2 indicate that motor slowing is a gradual process which depends inherently on the initial speed and the time it is maintained.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the results from experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Motor slowing exhibits two hallmark features of performance fatigability as demonstrated previously for tasks impacting strongly on peripheral neuromuscular factors.
source: Thus, motor slowing exhibits two hallmark features of performance fatigability as demonstrated previously for tasks impacting strongly on peripheral neuromuscular factors, for example, sustained isometric contractions at high force levels (Enoka and Stuart, 1992).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and comparison to previous literature.

claim: All tasks (foot tapping, eye movements, finger tapping) caused significant motor slowing of about 20% over a period of 30 s.
source: All tasks caused significant motor slowing of about 20% over a period of 30 s (foot: 13.9 ± 2.7% Cohen's d = 1.88; eyes: 18.3 ± 2.8%, Cohen's d = 3.35; finger: 21.6 ± 6.4% Cohen's d = 2.48, all values mean ± sem; linear mixed-effects model (LMEM) summarised results for experiments 1–3; F(2,11) ≥21.813, p<=0.001, Figure 2B–D.).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from experiments 3-5 with statistical analysis.

claim: There was virtually no accumulation of motor slowing over the course of the experiment, that is the initial tapping speed measured during the first 10 s of each trial was largely unchanged.
source: Interestingly, we observed virtually no accumulation of motor slowing over the course of the experiment, that is the initial tapping speed measured during the first 10 s of each trial was largely unchanged (see Table 1; time effect: p≥0.134).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Table 1.

claim: The process causing motor slowing is able to spontaneously recover during the subsequent 30 s break.
source: This suggests that the process causing motor slowing is able to spontaneously recover during the subsequent 30 s break.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that initial tapping speed does not accumulate across trials.

claim: Break length had a strong influence on the initial tapping speed (0–10 s), but not the final tapping speed (20–30 s).
source: This demonstrates that break length had a strong influence on the initial tapping speed (0–10 s), but not the final tapping speed (20–30 s).
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of experiment 5 where break length was varied.

claim: Longer breaks lead to more recovery than shorter breaks.
source: We found a significant condition × break length interaction (LMEM, F(5,16)=8.771, p<0.001, Figure 3D) indicating that longer breaks lead to more recovery than shorter breaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of recovery data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the average amount of slowing observed for an individual participant and the slope of recovery during the break.
source: Finally, there was a significant correlation between the average amount of slowing observed for an individual participant and the slope of recovery during the break (n = 17, Pearson r = 0.7543, p<0.001, Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Motor slowing occurs during prolonged tapping at maximal movement speeds irrespective of which effector or tapping task is performed.
source: In summary, our behavioural results show that motor slowing occurs during prolonged tapping at maximal movement speeds irrespective of which effector or tapping task is performed.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on experiments 3-5 testing different effectors.

claim: Less motor slowing is observed when movements are performed at slower speeds or for shorter durations.
source: Less motor slowing is observed when movements are performed at slower speeds or for shorter durations.
evidence: This is based on the findings from experiments 1 and 2.

claim: The mechanism which causes slowing for fast, long-lasting repetitive movements appears to quickly recover during the subsequent 25–30 s break following an approximately linear time course.
source: However, our data also suggest that the mechanism which causes slowing for fast, long-lasting repetitive movements appears to quickly recover during the subsequent 25–30 s break following an approximately linear time course.
evidence: This is based on the recovery data from experiment 5.

claim: Participants exhibited significant motor slowing in the MR scanner with a similar effect size to that observed during the behavioural experiment.
source: In the MR scanner, the participants exhibited significant motor slowing (Figure 4C) with a similar effect size to that observed during the behavioural experiment above (F(2,48)=85.557, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.98).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data collected during the fMRI experiment (experiment 6).

claim: Tapping with the right (dominant) hand activated a typical sensorimotor network, including left primary sensorimotor cortex (SM1), bilateral dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), right cerebellum lobule HVI (Cb), left posterior putamen (Put), left ventrolateral thalamus (Tha), and bilateral secondary somatosensory cortex (S2).
source: Tapping with the right (dominant) hand activated a typical sensorimotor network (Figure 4B, purple; Supplementary file 2), including left primary sensorimotor cortex (SM1), bilateral dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), bilateral supplementary motor area (SMA), right cerebellum lobule HVI (Cb), left posterior putamen (Put), left ventrolateral thalamus (Tha), and bilateral secondary somatosensory cortex (S2).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data from experiment 6 shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All motor areas showed a trend towards an activation increase even though tapping speed decreased due to motor slowing, but this effect only reached significance for voxels in contralateral SM1, PMd and SMA.
source: We found that all motor areas showed a trend towards an activation increase even though tapping speed decreased due to motor slowing. However, this effect only reached significance for voxels in contralateral SM1, PMd and SMA (Figure 4B, blue; Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI parametric analysis from experiment 6.

claim: Areas in SM1, PMd, SMA, ipsilateral cerebellar motor lobules (HVI) and contralateral S2 showed decreasing activity over the course of recovery which was significantly larger after the slowing condition than after the control condition.
source: We found a significant effect of recovery for voxels in SM1, PMd, SMA (pFWE <0.05; Figure 4B,D,E green). Additionally, we found increased activation in the ipsilateral cerebellar motor lobules (HVI) and contralateral S2 associated with recovery during the break. All of these areas showed decreasing activity over the course of recovery which was significantly larger after the slowing condition than after the control condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI recovery analysis from experiment 6.

claim: A reduction in tapping speed during the slowing condition was associated with an activation increase in the motor network which gradually normalised during the subsequent recovery period.
source: Thus, somewhat counterintuitively, our fMRI analyses revealed that a reduction in tapping speed during the slowing condition was associated with (i) an activation increase in the motor network which (ii) gradually normalised during the subsequent recovery period.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI findings from experiment 6.

claim: For SM1 (but not PMd and SMA), event-related power synchronisation in the alpha band was more strongly decreased immediately after the slowing condition than after the control condition.
source: For SM1 (but not PMd and SMA), we found that event-related power synchronisation in the alpha band (Pfurtscheller et al., 1996) was more strongly decreased immediately after the slowing condition than after the control condition (Figure 5D, green vs. red).
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data from experiment 7 shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Alpha-power was significantly lower during the first two time bins (0–10 s and 10–20 s) of the recovery period after the slowing condition than after the control condition.
source: We found a significant condition x time interaction (F(2,1136) = 3.195,p=0.041) for left SM1. Post-hoc comparisons revealed that alpha-power was significantly lower during the first two time bins (0–10 s and 10–20 s) of the recovery period after the slowing condition than after the control condition (puncorr <0.05), confirming that alpha power recovered more quickly after the control condition than after the slowing condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EEG data from experiment 7.

claim: No such differences in the time course of recovery were observed for the beta or gamma band.
source: No such differences in the time course of recovery were observed for the beta or gamma band.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the EEG analysis in experiment 7.

claim: Low alpha power within the sensorimotor system is associated with an elevated BOLD signal.
source: Our EEG results are consistent with the fMRI findings (see above) since it has been shown that low alpha power within the sensorimotor system is associated with an elevated BOLD signal (Bächinger et al., 2017; Hipp et al., 2012; Ritter et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activity in the alpha band reflects top-down inhibitory control processes.
source: In line with these findings, it has been proposed that activity in the alpha band reflects top-down inhibitory control processes (Klimesch et al., 2007) suggesting that low alpha power - as observed in SM1 immediately after the slowing condition - reflects a prominent release of inhibition which gradually recovered over the time course of the break.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and used to interpret the EEG findings.

claim: There was a significant decrease of the movement speed during the slowing condition in the SICI experiment.
source: Again, there was a significant decrease of the movement speed during the slowing condition (F(3,36)=42.94, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 2.40; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from experiment 8.

claim: SICI was strongly decreased immediately after the motor slowing condition (0–10 s of recovery period) as compared to both the Pre and Post measurements, but returned back to baseline at the end of the recovery period (20–30 s).
source: More specifically, SICI was strongly decreased immediately after the motor slowing condition (0–10 s of recovery period) as compared to both the Pre and Post measurements. However, it returned back to baseline at the end of the recovery period (20–30 s) (Figure 6C, green bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by TMS SICI measurements from experiment 8 shown in Figure 6C.

claim: After the control condition, SICI was only slightly decreased and recovered almost immediately after tapping.
source: By contrast, after the control condition, SICI was only slightly decreased and recovered almost immediately after tapping (Figure 6C, red bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by TMS SICI measurements from experiment 8 shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Performing repetitive movements for a period of ≥ 30 s leads to a strong release of inhibition within SM1 that gradually normalised over time.
source: Thus, in line with the fMRI and EEG findings reported above, the TMS experiment revealed further evidence that performing repetitive movements for a period of ≥ 30 s leads to a strong release of inhibition within SM1 that gradually normalised over time.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the SICI findings from experiment 8.

claim: There was a significant increase in coactivation over the course of tapping.
source: We found a significant increase in coactivation over the course of tapping (Figure 7C, F(2 and 36)=9.915, p=0.001), and over the course of motor slowing, changes in coactivation in a single participant was directly related to his/her changes in movement speed (LMEM, F(1,1561.414) = 4.243, p=0.040).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG coactivation analysis from experiment 9 shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Changes in coactivation in a single participant was directly related to his/her changes in movement speed.
source: We found a significant increase in coactivation over the course of tapping (Figure 7C, F(2 and 36)=9.915, p=0.001), and over the course of motor slowing, changes in coactivation in a single participant was directly related to his/her changes in movement speed (LMEM, F(1,1561.414) = 4.243, p=0.040).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of EMG data from experiment 9.

claim: Normalised surround inhibition measured during the first 10 s of the recovery phase was significantly decreased for the slowing condition compared to the control condition, but reached similar levels at the end of the break.
source: To compare the results between the two sessions we normalised surround inhibition measurements obtained during the break to the individual Pre measurements. Normalised surround inhibition measured during the first 10 s of the recovery phase was significantly decreased for the slowing condition compared to the control condition, but reached similar levels at the end of the break (significant condition x time interaction (Figure 7E; F(2,18) = 3.908, p=0.039)).
evidence: This claim is supported by TMS surround inhibition measurements from experiment 9 shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Individuals with a high coactivation index exhibit a strong release of surround inhibition.
source: Further, across participants, the average amount of coactivation in the last 10 s of slowing trials was predictive of the average amount of surround inhibition measured early during the recovery period such that individuals with a high coa index exhibit a strong release of surround inhibition (Figure 7F; linear regression model; R2 = 0.228, p=0.039).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The amount of motor slowing, the amount of coactivation between the agonistic and antagonistic muscle, and the strong release of surround inhibition are associated.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the amount of motor slowing, the amount of coactivation between the agonistic and antagonistic muscle, and the strong release of surround inhibition are associated.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the findings from experiment 9.

claim: Fast repetitive movements cause an increase of the excitation-inhibition ratio at the level of M1 which results, at least partly, from a breakdown of surround inhibition.
source: We therefore propose that fast repetitive movements cause an increase of the excitation-inhibition ratio at the level of M1 which results, at least partly, from a breakdown of surround inhibition.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings from experiment 9.

claim: Coactivation of agonistic and antagonistic muscles increases, which ultimately leads to a decrease in movement speed as observed during motor slowing.
source: Accordingly, coactivation of agonistic and antagonistic muscles increases, which ultimately leads to a decrease in movement speed as observed during motor slowing.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: An abnormal release of inhibition within SM1 might be related to pathological fatigability and/or bradykinetic movements.
source: Even though we tested healthy participants, it is possible that motor slowing shares mechanistic similarities with pathological forms of fatigue that are frequently observed in neurological patients (Lewis and Wessely, 1992; Lou, 2009; Ranjith, 2005; Watanabe et al., 2008). Our study provides the testable hypothesis that an abnormal release of inhibition within SM1 might be related to pathological fatigability and/or bradykinetic movements.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental findings and citations to clinical literature.

claim: Neurons in primary motor cortex are tuned to represent movement direction in extrinsic space.
source: It is well known that neurons in primary motor cortex are tuned to represent movement direction in extrinsic space (Georgopoulos and Carpenter, 2015; Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Georgopoulos et al., 1986) and that this tuning is sculpted by inhibitory mechanisms (Merchant et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Circuits mediating local inhibition lead to a sharpening of the directional tuning curve, which determines the accuracy of the directional motor command.
source: In particular, it has been proposed that circuits mediating local inhibition lead to a sharpening of the directional tuning curve, which determines the accuracy of the directional motor command (Mahan and Georgopoulos, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: When fast tapping needs to be maintained over a longer period of time, surround inhibition breaks down and the tuning curves of both populations become broader.
source: However, when the fast tapping needs to be maintained over a longer period of time, surround inhibition breaks down and the tuning curves of both populations become broader (Figure 8; right side).
evidence: This is part of the proposed theoretical model illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The descending motor command is less accurate making the muscle activation pattern less efficient activating antagonistic muscle groups in parallel.
source: In turn, the descending motor command is less accurate making the muscle activation pattern less efficient activating antagonistic muscle groups in parallel.
evidence: This is part of the proposed theoretical model.

claim: Brain activity increases during fatiguing isometric contractions.
source: This model might also explain why brain activity increases during fatiguing isometric contractions (van Duinen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and used to support the proposed model.

claim: Isometric contractions can be maintained longer when an external focus of attention is adopted.
source: In line with this proposal, it has been shown that isometric contractions can be maintained longer when an external focus of attention is adopted (Kuhn et al., 2017a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Improvement of performance during external focus of attention was accompanied by an increase in SICI and an increase in surround inhibition.
source: Interestingly, this improvement of performance was accompanied by an increase in SICI (Kuhn et al., 2017a; Kuhn et al., 2017b) and an increase in surround inhibition (Kuhn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fast repetitive movements are subject to gradual slowing even though each single muscle contraction is brief and submaximal.
source: Here we show that fast repetitive movements are subject to gradual slowing even though each single muscle contraction is brief and submaximal.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on all the behavioral experiments.

claim: Motor slowing arises from transient neurophysiological changes of supraspinal areas indicating that this form of motor fatigability is largely mediated by central mechanisms.
source: Based on converging evidence from behavioural, fMRI, EEG and TMS measurements we argue that motor slowing arises from transient neurophysiological changes of supraspinal areas indicating that this form of motor fatigability is largely mediated by central mechanisms.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Motor slowing is accompanied by a gradual shift of the excitation-inhibition balance within primary motor cortex towards more net excitation.
source: Specifically, we show that motor slowing is accompanied by a gradual shift of the excitation-inhibition balance within primary motor cortex towards more net excitation.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the fMRI, EEG, and TMS findings.

claim: This shift results from the release of inhibition in M1 and, particularly, the breakdown of surround inhibition causing increased cocontraction between antagonistic muscle groups which, in turn, leads to more and more effortful and slow tapping movements.
source: Even though paradoxical at first, we show that this shift results from the release of inhibition in M1 and, particularly, the breakdown of surround inhibition causing increased cocontraction between antagonistic muscle groups which, in turn, leads to more and more effortful and slow tapping movements.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental findings, particularly from experiment 9.

claim: A breakdown of surround inhibition causes a broader tuning of neuronal populations in M1 that encode movement direction, resulting in a sub-optimal and less efficient descending motor command than at the beginning of tapping.
source: We further propose a model in which this breakdown of surround inhibition causes a broader tuning of neuronal populations in M1 that encode movement direction, resulting in a sub-optimal and less efficient descending motor command than at the beginning of tapping.
evidence: This is the proposed theoretical model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Motor slowing is not only generalisable across muscle groups and tasks, but is also present in almost all participants, reflecting a fundamental control principle of the brain.
source: Given that motor slowing is not only generalisable across muscle groups and tasks, but is also present in almost all participants, it reflects a fundamental control principle of the brain suggesting that inhibitory control is essential for high motor efficiency and that a breakdown of inhibition results in more and more effortful movements.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the generalizability of the findings across experiments.

claim: Inhibitory control is essential for high motor efficiency and a breakdown of inhibition results in more and more effortful movements.
source: Given that motor slowing is not only generalisable across muscle groups and tasks, but is also present in almost all participants, it reflects a fundamental control principle of the brain suggesting that inhibitory control is essential for high motor efficiency and that a breakdown of inhibition results in more and more effortful movements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The BOLD signal has poor temporal resolution.
source: It is well-known that the BOLD signal has poor temporal resolution and, thus, we cannot exclude that the effects observed during the recovery period were driven by inaccuracies in modelling the individual hemodynamic response function (Balsters and Ramnani, 2011; Handwerker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a known limitation of fMRI supported by citations.

claim: High alpha-activity has been suggested to reflect inhibitory activity.
source: High alpha-activity has been suggested to reflect inhibitory activity (Klimesch et al., 2007), thereby providing indirect evidence that motor slowing is associated with a pronounced release of SM1 inhibition, which is gradually restored during the subsequent break.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SICI measurements assess the activity of GABAA-ergic networks within M1.
source: These EEG results were further supported by SICI measurements that assess the activity of GABAA-ergic networks within M1 (Werhahn et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The increase in BOLD signal is likely to reflect higher net excitation of the motor network, resulting from a shift of the excitation-inhibition balance towards excitation.
source: Under the assumption that these after-effects of reduced inhibition are representative of neurophysiological changes underpinning the motor slowing phenomenon during movement execution, the increase in BOLD signal is likely to reflect higher net excitation of the motor network (Waldvogel et al., 2000), resulting from a shift of the excitation-inhibition balance towards excitation (Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and citations to previous literature.

claim: Repetitive single joint movements require the sequential activity of agonistic and antagonistic muscles.
source: Repetitive single joint movements require the sequential activity of agonistic and antagonistic muscles.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about motor control.

claim: The ability to selectively activate one specific muscle while suppressing unwanted activity in other muscles requires surround inhibition.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that the ability to selectively activate one specific muscle while suppressing unwanted activity in other muscles requires surround inhibition (Beck and Hallett, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The change in BOLD signal in S1/M1, premotor cortex, SMA, thalamus and selected basal ganglia nuclei is higher for high levels of force production compared to low levels of force production.
source: More specifically, the change in BOLD signal in S1/M1, premotor cortex, SMA, thalamus and selected basal ganglia nuclei is higher for high levels of force production compared to low levels of force production (Spraker et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Performing passive movements with increasing velocity causes a linear increase in the BOLD signal in S1/M1, secondary somatosensory cortex (S2), and SMA.
source: Similarly, performing passive movements with increasing velocity causes a linear increase in the BOLD signal in S1/M1, secondary somatosensory cortex (S2), and SMA, which corresponds well to the rate encoding principles shown for sensory afferent signals (Dueñas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Previous work demonstrated increasing activity in SM1, PMd and SMA during fatiguing maximal isometric contractions, as characterised by a progressive decline in maximal finger abduction force.
source: However, our finding is in line with previous work demonstrating increasing activity in SM1, PMd and SMA during fatiguing maximal isometric contractions, as characterised by a progressive decline in maximal finger abduction force (Post et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: During fatiguing contractions, the amplitude of the superimposed twitch increases gradually suggesting that the central drive is insufficient to maintain truly maximal contractions.
source: This has been shown by the 'superimposed twitch' method, that is applying electrical stimulation which evokes an increment in force (Gandevia et al., 1996; Schillings et al., 2003). During fatiguing contractions, the amplitude of the superimposed twitch increases gradually suggesting that, despite the observed increase in the BOLD signal of cortical motor areas, the central drive is insufficient to maintain truly maximal contractions (Post et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Event-related alpha synchronisation does not differ between long versus short isometric contractions.
source: Moreover, event-related alpha synchronisation does not differ between long versus short isometric contractions (Cassim et al., 2000), therefore, the differential dynamics of alpha-band activity in our EEG study are unlikely the result of different movement durations for the motor slowing versus the (less-slowing) control condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and used to rule out an alternative explanation.

claim: Central fatigability has been conceptualised as a decrease in voluntary drive, resulting in descending motor commands that are insufficient to maintain high tapping speed or high isometric muscle contractions.
source: Central fatigability has been conceptualised as a decrease in voluntary drive, resulting in descending motor commands that are insufficient to maintain high tapping speed or high isometric muscle contractions (Gandevia et al., 1996; Kluger et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: For isometric contractions, performance fatigability is defined as a gradual reduction in output force that strongly depends on the initial force level and the duration it must be maintained.
source: For isometric contractions, performance fatigability is defined as a gradual reduction in output force that strongly depends on the initial force level and the duration it must be maintained (Taylor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The systematic reduction of force output over time is strongest if initial target force levels are high but depends predominantly on peripheral factors.
source: Importantly, the systematic reduction of force output over time is strongest if initial target force levels are high but depends predominantly on peripheral factors (Place et al., 2010; Enoka and Stuart, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Supraspinal mechanisms are the main contributors to motor slowing as investigated here, since it causes neither a change in isometric maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) force, nor a change in force production evoked by electrical stimulation of the muscle.
source: More specifically, it has been suggested that supraspinal mechanisms are the main contributors to motor slowing as investigated here, since it causes neither a change in isometric maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) force, nor a change in force production evoked by electrical stimulation of the muscle (Arias et al., 2015; Madrid et al., 2018; Miller et al., 1993; Rodrigues et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.
